newsitem.title: TANZANIA: U.S. envoy, African heads meet to discuss Burundi.
newsitem.headline: U.S. envoy, African heads meet to discuss Burundi.

text.p: African leaders and U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher gather in this northern Tanzanian town on Friday to review the crisis in war-torn Burundi, but the country's main players will be absent.

Presidents Benjamin Mkapa of Tanzania, Yoweri Museveni of Uganda and Daniel arap Moi of Kenya will meet Christopher and discuss issues ranging from regional economic cooperation to ethnic violence in Burundi and Rwanda and a potentially explosive situation in eastern Zaire.

After Christopher's departure for South Africa, the three presidents will be joined by counterparts from Rwanda, Zambia, Ethiopia, Zairean Premier Kengo wa Dondo and officials of the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) at talks to review the crippling economic embargo imposed on Burundi in July.

At a meeting with Christopher on Friday, the three African leaders, to be joined later by Burundi mediator and former Tanzanian president Julius Nyerere, will seek American support for the East African Cooperation organisation, revived a few years ago to boost regional integration.
But diplomats in Arusha for Friday's meeting concede Christopher's talks will be dominated by ethnic violence in Burundi -- claiming 1,000 lives monthly and over 150,000 in the past three years.

"Whichever way you look at it, this meeting will have to be dominated by Burundi. It would be foolish to discuss regional economic progress in the light of an explosive situation in Burundi," a European diplomat told Reuters.
Diplomats said Christopher's presence could well help take decisions essential for progress at a full-scale African summit on Burundi on Saturday.

First, the question of Burundi's military strongman Major Pierre Buyoya's presence at the summit still hangs in the air. Buyoya is an ethnic Tutsi who seized power in a bloodless coup in July after ousting ethnic Hutu president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya.

Also undecided is whether the Hutu rebels fighting Buyoya's army will be represented. The main one is the National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD), led by former interior minister Leonard Nyangoma.

Diplomats said Tanzania, the driving force behind a regional economic embargo on Burundi, would like Buyoya to attend as a faction leader and not head of state. Buyoya insists on attending only as president.

"We have asked to be invited as head of state of Burundi. It is clear I will not go unless it is as head of state of Burundi," Buyoya told a news conference in the Burundi capital Bujumbura on Thursday.

Diplomats said the regional African gathering was divided between those who want Buyoya to be invited to the summit unconditionally and those insisting he comes only as a faction leader at the helm of his country's Tutsi-dominated army.

Regional analysts said Christopher's presence in Arusha, where he will also visit the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the East African Cooperation Secretariat, could help break the impasse on Buyoya's position.
"He may just be the right guy to resolve the dilemma on the Burundi summit and give it a positive push forward," an African ambassador told Reuters.

Regional analysts fear that Burundi, riven by war between the Tutsi-dominated army and Hutu rebels, could go down the same path as neighbouring Rwanda, where a million Tutsis and politically moderate Hutus were slaughtered in 1994.
At the end of the Arusha talks, the presidents will have to take a tough decision -- whether to lift the sanctions imposed on Burundi, ease them or further tighten them.

Burundi says the sanctions cost it more than $130 million in the first two months. Worst hit are workers and residents of Bujumbura, now an eerie town abandoned by majority Hutus who have fled to the countryside.

Buyoya's junta last month lifted its ban on political parties, restored parliament and agreed in principle to meet Hutu rebels, waging a ferocious war in the tiny tea and coffee-growing central African nation.
In so doing, Buyoya and his military colleagues believe they have gone far enough in responding to demands imposed by regional countries after his overthrow of Ntibantunganya.
